Candidate A splits after the comma: LEFT = "A geologist finishes a week of desert field work," RIGHT = "then three months later begins laboratory analysis in another city."

Candidate B splits before the comma: LEFT = "A geologist finishes a week of desert field work, then three months later" RIGHT = "begins laboratory analysis in another city."

Which is better? The phrase "then three months later" modifies the second clause. In Candidate A, it's part of right side; left ends with just first clause. That seems fine: two independent clauses separated by comma and conjunction 'then'. But we have a comma before then. Actually original has comma after field work, then "three months later". So splitting at that comma yields left as first clause, right starting with "then three months later begins...".

Candidate B includes the time phrase in left side; right is just verb phrase. That seems less natural: "begins laboratory analysis" alone? Might be okay but missing subject? Subject implied geologist. But it's fine.

Large-chapter split likely wants each unit to have a complete clause with subject and predicate. Candidate A's right has subject implicit, but still a clause. Candidate B left also is a clause; right is just verb phrase lacking explicit subject but could be considered part of the same sentence? Might be less balanced.

Thus choose A. Provide reason: splits into two independent clauses each with clear subject/predicate and time marker on second side.
